Of course with no knowledge of the facts of the case, except as stated in the letter and the reply. with no acquaintance with the condition of the farm, at entry and lon leaving, without the bills and vouchers for improvements being before us, we must' speak with reserve, and although we are in- clined to suspect that in this cue the land- lord is right and the tenant is wrong, yet none the less do the oircumatanoes prove how much more satisfactory it would have been, had there been some means of obtaining an authoritative decision as to the amount due on one side, and the improvements made on the other. Now, no one who knows Cheshire 'and Cheshire landlords, will for a moment suspect that the Duke of Weritininster wished to act harshly in the case. Equally I plain is it that if in any case a landlord is entitled to do what he likes with his own land, it is when that land is part of hie de. mane, and eurr. ,unded by his woods and ornamental plantations. And en an estate of the magnitude of the Duke of Westminster, it is, we take it, far more for the interest of the landlord to establish a spirit of confidence in the body of the tenantry, than to snatch a paltry advantage by a bit of sharp prac- tice. Nay more, we know that for many years in the time of the late Marquis, and probably even now, the whole income of the Cheshire and Flintahire estates haa been spent in improvements, which of course is only possible in the case of a man who has other source:, of income than agricultural land. no that from a review of the general management of an estate, and the excep- tional circumstances of the farm, we shbuld say that the landlord was clearly entitled to recover possession of the farm if for any cause he thought it desirable to do so, pay- ing of course what was due to the tenant for unexhausted improvements. People are apt to talk and to think as if there were only two parties in- terested in the culture of the soil, the land- lord and the tenant. To our mind there are two other classes equally interested, the agricultural labourers and the general publio. The former depends on the proper culture of the soil for his (lady bread, and his wages are raised and lowered by the amount of labour expended in agricultural matters. A man is told to leave his farm, and at once charges his landlord and his landlord's servants with spite, conspiracy and fraud, simply because the relations between land- lords and tenants are by our precious land' laws, such that no one can safely interpret , them or satisfactorily clear them up. A man who receive notice to quit a house or a mill may grumble at the trouble and incon- venience, but ha knows that is legal rights are safe and definite, and that he will not leave the value of a Id. behind him.
